attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' with no hedge, so it is a scorable forecast. The budget-cut qualifier and the 20-student TA sections are kept. No deadline was given.

contract.note: The plain reading (affordability, not adoption; 'few' means a small minority; US as the main population) is fair and ordinary. The early-resolution rule sensibly requires a representative capacity study.

evidence.note: Sacramento State's own disclosure of cuts made for budget reasons. It bears on the antecedent at one campus, not on how many universities can afford TA sections.
National SHEEO data from before the cutoff: per-student funding fell a little while total appropriations rose. Says nothing about the affordable share.

reviews.rationale: Firm forecast with no deadline. The packet has no representative capacity study or funded sector-wide rollout, so the early-resolution rule is not met. The evidence covers the budget-cut condition and national funding context only, not how many universities could afford 20-student TA sections.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'All of this' correctly points to the three term-paper functions. 'Nuked' is read as destroyed, which matches the firm metaphor.

contract.note: Reading 'nuked' as largely destroying these functions in ordinary term papers is the ordinary reading, stretched neither way. The period from ChatGPT's launch to the post is reasonable.

evidence.note: One small MBA class with a redesigned assignment, measuring perceived usefulness. Not ordinary term papers, and not at scale.
Shows AI submissions to take-home exams went largely undetected, so assessment is vulnerable. Does not measure term papers, writing practice or reflection.

reviews.rationale: Neither item is the comparative evidence the contract requires. e2 shows exam assessment is vulnerable but does not cover term papers or the other two functions. e1 is a small redesigned case. Neither near-total destruction nor substantial persistence is established.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Firm present-tense claim that term papers are now basically worthless. Adding 'because of GenAI' matches the surrounding context.

contract.note: Reading it as ordinary take-home term papers having lost nearly all practical value in large classes is fair and ordinary. Using the 2024-25 academic year is a disclosed convention.

evidence.note: UK survey from December 2024 showing widespread AI use for assessments, mostly as study help. Measures uptake, not the remaining value of term papers.

reviews.rationale: The only item measures how widely students use AI, not the learning or assessment value of term papers in large classes, or their staffing costs. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own rhetorical question, which carries an assertion he endorses.

semantics.note: The question presupposes as fact that GenAI's makers and distributors caused the problem. Widening 'this huge problem' to the broader education harm matches the context.

contract.note: Whether 'huge problem' means assessment vulnerability alone or broad learning loss decides the result. The contract flags this and picks the broader reading, which the context supports. That is fair.

evidence.note: Supports the narrower point: AI-written exam answers mostly went undetected and outscored real students. Does not show widespread deterioration.
Preprint dated before the cutoff finding small grade and satisfaction effects. Its data run past the post, and grades are not direct measures of learning.

reviews.rationale: e1 supports only the assessment-vulnerability part, which the contract says is not enough. e2 tempers the broad harm claim but is not decisive for the period. Widespread causal deterioration is neither shown nor refuted.
